claims.text: Current Kotlin documentation defines a coroutine as a suspendable computation, states that on JVM and Kotlin/Native concurrent code including coroutines runs on operating-system-managed threads, explains that suspension can release a thread to run another coroutine, and states that a dispatcher controls which thread or thread pool executes a coroutine.

Current Kotlin documentation describes structured concurrency as a parent-child task tree: a parent waits for children, and parent failure or cancellation recursively cancels children. The candidate correctly uses this as the ordinary scope boundary rather than claiming every supervisor relationship behaves identically.

The kotlinx.coroutines 1.11.0 supervisorScope API states that a child failure does not affect other children, while an exception from the supervisorScope block cancels the scope and its children. The candidate states this boundary accurately.

The kotlinx.coroutines 1.11.0 runBlocking API states that runBlocking blocks the current thread until completion, is intended as a bridge from regular blocking code to suspending libraries, and is redundant/blocking inside suspend functions. Kotlin dispatcher documentation also describes shared thread pools and CPU-oriented Dispatchers.Default, supporting the candidate boundary that coroutine count does not create extra CPU parallelism.

findings: Both duplicate source rows ask the same concept comparison; the stale generated scenario context was repaired to concept.
The candidate explicitly limits implementation-specific claims to Kotlin/JVM instead of universalizing coroutine internals across languages.

Suspension versus thread blocking, dispatcher/thread ownership, structured concurrency, supervisorScope isolation, and runBlocking behavior all match current Kotlin/kotlinx.coroutines 1.11.0 documentation.
The answer correctly bounds the high-concurrency advantage to suspendable waiting and does not claim that more coroutines create more CPU parallelism or make arbitrary blocking APIs nonblocking.
